title: Oldest quasar discovered tightens black hole formulation theories
excerpt: A 630 million year old quasar, first identified in the EWS, has raised new questions about the size and formulation of its origins
content:
A team of astronomers led by Julien Wolf, a postdoc at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy, discovered the most distant quasar to date, with a cosmic age of 630 million years after the Big Bang.

Redshift was used to gauge the age of the quasar, formally identified as J1504+6252 and nicknamed ‘Dún Aonghasa’ by the team. This measures how much of the wavelength of the light emitted at the source has been stretched by cosmic expansion by the point at which it reaches the telescope. Sometimes this redshift can be interpreted as a distance, although no quasar has ever been found to have a redshift greater than eight.

Corroborated by a variety of observatories, such as W.M. Keck Observatory, the Hubble Space Telescope, the Large Binocular Telescope and ultimately the James Webb Space Telescope, the quasar was found to be 40 million years older than the previous oldest quasar on record- and had a redshift of z = 8.13.

Quasars are incredibly bright galaxy cores with supermassive black holes in a feeding phase, with nearby material pulled into a turbulent swirl of gas that heats up and glows brighter than entire galaxies before collapsing into the black hole.

Despite being billions of years old, the persistent brightness of quasars mean they are a valuable point of study for learning about the earliest epochs of the Universe.

Dún Aonghasa’s size and age makes it especially notable in this regard, with a supermassive black hole with a mass of several hundred million times the Sun.

“Finding quasars at ever-increasing distances, at the edge of the observable universe, teaches us something about how the black holes in their centres grew,” says Julien Wolf. “The closer to the Big Bang we find them, the faster their black holes must have grown or the more massive they must have been at birth — or both.” This puts strict constraints on the mechanisms that helped increase their masses so vastly and quickly.

Using established theories and observational data, the team computed under which circumstances the proposed scenarios could produce black holes as massive as the one powering Dún Aonghasa.

Considering reasonable growth rates, the latest discoveries seem to be consistent with a direct collapse scenario, in which a massive gas cloud condenses under its own gravity and directly forms a black hole which subsequently continues to grow. The growth rate is usually limited by a self-regulating mechanism that, at increasingly high temperatures, repels the collapsing gas, commonly labelled the Eddington limit.

Interestingly, observational data indicate that Dún Aonghasa is growing far below that limit, which shows that even the most distant quasars collect gas at varying rates. If this quasar had always grown this slowly, it would have required an extremely massive initial seed, which is difficult to explain with current formation models. Instead, an early black hole as massive as Dún Aonghasa supports the idea of a much more rapid accretion in the past, perhaps even beyond the theoretical Eddington limit.

Altogether, the conditions for a direct collapse to happen must have been rare during this era of cosmic evolution, which could explain the few quasars found at redshifts beyond 7.5 so far. If, at some point, astronomers discover quasars at considerably higher redshifts, i.e. approaching a cosmic age of just a few hundred million years, even the direct collapse scenario may become less likely.

In this case, astronomers may have to consider yet another, more exotic alternative: primordial black holes – hypothetical black holes formed right after the Big Bang which would function as massive seeds for gas to accumulate. Even without requiring extreme growth rates, such massive objects would provide a head start, giving the black holes ample time to gain weight worth millions upon millions of solar masses. Only future observations and discoveries of perhaps even more distant quasars will fully resolve the puzzle of how they formed.
